topicCandidates: A practical framework separating five language layers: the communication actually needed for the job, an employer's screening preference, an immigration or program criterion, a regulated-profession or examination rule, and evidence that demonstrates a particular skill.

The Japanese-Language Proficiency Test from N5 through N1, including what its language-knowledge, reading, and listening scores can support; its lack of speaking and writing tests; the score-based CEFR reference indication introduced from the December 2025 test; and the difference between certificate validity and an employer's recency policy.

The Japan Foundation Test for Basic Japanese as an assessment of everyday-life communication for people mainly coming to work, including its specific use in Specified Skilled Worker and other named procedures without presenting it as proof of advanced workplace Japanese.

Business Japanese Language Test evidence where a current immigration framework expressly recognizes a score, while keeping that legal use distinct from an employer's own assessment of meetings, email, negotiation, technical vocabulary, and customer communication.

Occupation-sensitive examples for software and engineering, design and creative work, research and academia, office and sales work, hospitality and customer service, teaching, skilled-sector work, nursing care, and licensed medical professions.

English-language requirements in Japan, distinguishing an employer's phrases such as native, native-level, fluent, or business English from the Instructor status evidence, private-company language-instruction criteria, JET Programme rules, teaching qualifications, and proof of actual speaking or writing ability.

How applicants can read a job advertisement and verify the exact language tasks, accepted evidence, interview language, certificate recency, safety or customer-facing duties, and whether a stated level is required, preferred, or negotiable.

How employers can define proportionate, task-related language criteria, assess the abilities the work actually uses, and avoid treating nationality or an unrelated personal characteristic as a substitute for language competence.

Search and FAQ coverage for ordinary queries such as whether JLPT N2 is required for a developer, whether someone can work in Japan without Japanese, what native English means, and whether passing JLPT guarantees a job.
userSituations: A software engineer sees N2 in one vacancy and no Japanese requirement in another and assumes immigration law sets different rules for the same residence status.
A graphic designer has a strong portfolio but needs to determine whether briefs, critique, client meetings, production handoffs, and workplace tools will operate in Japanese or English.
A candidate who passed JLPT N1 assumes the certificate proves professional speaking, writing, negotiation, or field-specific vocabulary.
A candidate with strong spoken Japanese but no certificate needs to ask whether an employer accepts an interview, work sample, another test, or no formal evidence.
A person planning Specified Skilled Worker employment needs to identify the applicable Japanese test, field test, field-specific exception, and any additional nursing-care language assessment.
A foreign-trained nurse needs to distinguish an N1 examination-eligibility condition from the separate Japanese national examination, licence, employer, and residence-status requirements.
A Japanese university graduate considering Designated Activities No. 46 needs to verify the route's advanced-Japanese evidence rather than generalizing it to every graduate job.
A Highly Skilled Professional candidate wants to know when JLPT or BJT evidence can affect points without mistaking points for proof that the underlying work is authorized.

A founder assumes the revised Business Manager Japanese-capacity criterion must always be satisfied personally through JLPT, although the current rule can involve another qualifying person and a different proficiency framework.
An English-teaching applicant encounters native speaker, native-level, twelve years of education in English, TEFL, teaching licence, and Japanese ability across different vacancies and programs.
An employer wants to request Japanese ability that is genuinely necessary for safety, customers, records, supervision, or teamwork without using nationality as a proxy.
edgeCasesAndExceptions: JLPT currently tests language knowledge, reading, and listening, not conversation, speaking, composition, or writing. Its CEFR reference indication does not add productive or interactive skills to the test.
A JLPT certificate does not expire, but a company, school, or institution may impose its own recency rule. The reader must ask which document and test date the recipient accepts.
Passing a JLPT level does not guarantee that every successful examinee can perform every activity in the JLPT Can-do self-evaluation list or every task in a workplace.

An employer's N2 or N1 preference is not automatically an immigration requirement. Conversely, an employer waiving a certificate cannot waive an express immigration, program, examination, or licensing rule.

Specified Skilled Worker (i) generally requires the accepted Japanese and field skill tests unless an applicable exemption applies. Current exceptions include higher Japanese thresholds for specified transport or railway work and an additional language assessment for nursing care.

A Japanese-language threshold can belong to the person, another qualifying employee, a points calculation, a specific graduate route, an examination-eligibility process, or the work itself. These are not interchangeable.

Instructor evidence for teaching a foreign language can concern twelve years of education through that language. This is not the same statement as requiring citizenship, a native-speaker label, JLPT, TEFL, or a particular employer's hiring policy.

JET Programme ALT and CIR criteria differ: prior Japanese is not a universal ALT eligibility requirement, while the CIR role calls for functional Japanese at approximately JLPT N1 or N2. JET rules are program rules, not rules for every teaching job.
Private-company language teaching, covered school teaching, and university teaching can point to different residence statuses even when every employer calls the position English teacher.
TOEIC Listening and Reading does not directly demonstrate speaking and writing. If a job needs productive skills, the exact test module, interview, or work evidence matters.

Customer-facing, safety-critical, clinical, legal, managerial, and unsupervised duties can justify different practical language needs from an English-speaking engineering team, but job titles alone cannot determine the level.

A bilingual vacancy can still require Japanese for internal records, emergency instructions, clients, regulators, or later assignments. Applicants should verify the complete duty and communication environment rather than rely on the advertisement headline.
Nationality and language ability are different facts. Employer guidance should frame screening around aptitude and abilities necessary for the work rather than unrelated personal background.
jurisdictionVariables: The residence status, designated program, points route, professional licence, examination, and effective-dated criteria governing the proposed work.
The employer, occupation, actual duties, team language, customer contact, safety consequences, supervision, documentation, software, technical vocabulary, and future assignment expectations.
Whether the stated language level is mandatory, preferred, advantageous, or only one accepted form of evidence.
The tested language, test provider, test module, score or level, test date, certificate-recency policy, verification method, and skills the assessment does and does not measure.
For teaching work, the institution category, designated language, education through that language, teaching qualification, program rules, learner group, curriculum, and Japanese-language duties.
For regulated or sector work, the profession, field, licensing authority, skills test, language test, exemption, and additional field-specific communication assessment.
For remote, international, creative, and technical teams, the language of contracts, meetings, briefs, specifications, code or production review, client delivery, and workplace safety information.

contentImpacts.reason: Provide the canonical framework, credential explanations, profession examples, advertisement checklist, and legal-versus-employer boundaries planned by the Phase 13 coverage manifest.
Link language requirements as a separate hiring, program, licensing, or evidence layer rather than making language ability determine the work-status category.
Decode native-level wording, designated-language evidence, institution-specific status routes, JET differences, and Japanese-language expectations without creating one English-teacher rule.
Explain the official foreign-language education evidence and separate it from citizenship, JLPT, TEFL, teacher licensing, and employer preferences.

Add realistic language-task examples for IT, engineering, office, design, creative, translation, sales, and private-company language instruction while keeping language preferences separate from status eligibility.
Make the current general test route, field-specific N3 exceptions, nursing-care assessment, and exemptions easy to find without implying one level covers every field.
Link the language framework while retaining profession-specific licensing and foreign-trained nurse N1 context.
Clarify that the current B2-oriented capacity condition is not universally an applicant-held JLPT certificate.
Explain when JLPT or BJT can affect points without treating language points as the underlying work permission.
Expose the advanced-Japanese boundary for the relevant Japanese-university-graduate route without generalizing it across Designated Activities.
Define JLPT, its levels, tested skills, CEFR reference, validity, and common employment use.
Define the daily-life-focused test and its named procedural uses without presenting it as advanced business Japanese.
Define BJT and distinguish recognized immigration-score uses from an employer's wider communication assessment.
Add ordinary-language answers and search synonyms for JLPT levels, no-Japanese jobs, English teaching, certificates, and profession-specific exceptions.
Add the canonical guide to practical employment discovery while cross-linking it from Professional work rather than duplicating it.

scopeBoundaries: Do not publish one Japanese level as sufficient for all jobs, employers, workplaces, residence statuses, examinations, or licences.
Do not describe an employer's preferred JLPT level as immigration law, and do not imply that an employer can waive an express legal, program, or licensing criterion.
Do not claim that JLPT directly tests speaking or writing, that its CEFR reference covers productive skills, or that a pass guarantees a workplace task.
Do not convert rough phrases such as business Japanese, conversational Japanese, fluent, or native-level into unsupported score equivalencies.
Do not treat nationality, passport, birthplace, accent, or education country as automatically equivalent to language competence.
Do not give individualized discrimination findings or promise that a particular hiring criterion is lawful; provide the task-related fair-recruitment principle and an official help route.
Do not duplicate every residence-status or professional-licensing requirement in the canonical guide. Summarize the decision boundary and link to the current focused guide and authority.
Do not imply that a credential remains accepted merely because the certificate itself does not expire; the receiving organization can impose a current evidence policy.
Keep all new and materially revised content at needs-review until explicit human editorial approval.
unresolvedQuestions: Should BJT receive a glossary entry in the first implementation because current immigration frameworks recognize named scores, while TOEIC remains a contextual example rather than another glossary entry?
Should the canonical guide include a short employer-facing section on defining task-related language criteria, or should that be reserved for a later standalone recruitment guide?
Should the guide be added to both Working in Japan and Professional work while remaining optional context rather than a mandatory step in every work journey?

scopeApproval.note: The editor approved the canonical employment-language guide, immediate JLPT, JFT-Basic, and BJT glossary coverage, contextual rather than glossary-level TOEIC treatment, a concise employer-facing section, placement in Working in Japan with Professional work cross-links, and no mandatory journey step.
